Use only if clearly needed; limited data
Caution; small amounts excreted in milk

summary: Roxithromycin is a semisynthetic 14-membered macrolide antibacterial with improved acid stability and tissue penetration over erythromycin. It is active against Gram-positive cocci, atypical respiratory pathogens (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) and some Gram-negatives, and is used for respiratory, ENT, skin and genital infections. Usual adult dose is 150 mg twice daily or 300 mg once daily before food. Not FDA-approved.
indications: Upper respiratory tract infections (pharyngitis, tonsillitis, sinusitis)
Lower respiratory tract infections (bronchitis, community-acquired pneumonia including atypical pathogens)

dosage.d: 150 mg twice daily or 300 mg once daily

dosage.n: Use pediatric suspension per local label

admin: Take before meals, ideally on an empty stomach (15-30 minutes before food)
Complete the full prescribed course even if symptoms improve
Space dosing evenly to maintain tissue concentrations
moa: Roxithromycin binds reversibly to the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible bacteria, blocking the peptidyl transferase / translocation step of protein synthesis and inhibiting bacterial growth. It is predominantly bacteriostatic and concentrates well within phagocytes and tissues, contributing to activity against intracellular and atypical pathogens.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to roxithromycin or other macrolides
Concomitant drugs that prolong QT where macrolide adds risk (e.g. with terfenadine/astemizole historically)
relative: Concomitant CYP3A4 substrates with narrow index

preg: Not FDA-approved; manufacturer SmPC advises use during pregnancy only if clearly necessary as adequate controlled human data are limited. Avoid in the first trimester unless benefit outweighs risk.
lact: Small amounts are excreted in breast milk. Use with caution; consider stopping breastfeeding or the drug depending on importance to the mother.
renal: No dosage adjustment is generally required in mild to moderate renal impairment as elimination is predominantly biliary/fecal. Use with caution in severe impairment.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment as the drug is largely eliminated by the liver. In severe impairment a reduced dose (e.g. 150 mg once daily) and monitoring of liver function are advised.

major: Ergot alkaloids - risk of ergotism; contraindicated
Other QT-prolonging drugs - additive arrhythmia risk
moderate: Warfarin - increased anticoagulant effect; monitor INR
interactions.food: Food reduces absorption; take before meals.
interactions.diagnostics: No characteristic laboratory test interference; may transiently raise liver enzymes.

monitoring: Clinical response and resolution of infection
Liver function tests with prolonged therapy or pre-existing liver disease
ECG/QT and electrolytes in patients with cardiac risk factors
Signs of superinfection or C. difficile colitis with persistent diarrhea
counsel: Take before food on an empty stomach
Complete the full course; do not stop early
Report palpitations, fainting, severe diarrhea or yellowing of skin/eyes
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, especially ergot drugs and statins
pk: Store below 25 C; protect from moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved; pending clinical review. Widely licensed via EMA/SmPC and used per BNF.
Longer half-life than erythromycin allows once- or twice-daily dosing with better GI tolerance
Good intracellular and tissue penetration favors atypical respiratory pathogens
Lower CYP3A4 inhibition than erythromycin/clarithromycin but interactions still occur
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue the regular schedule; do not double the dose.
overdose: No specific antidote. Overdose may cause gastrointestinal upset and, with very high exposure, QT prolongation. Manage with supportive and symptomatic care, gastric decontamination if recent and large ingestion, and cardiac monitoring where indicated.
